samples.text: After one terrible conversation, I can see why you'd want to make a call about the person right then. Then sometimes they come back later and actually talk about what you were trying to say. They still disagree. Their boundary is still exactly the one you hated. But you're talking about the thing now. So what, exactly, did the first fight prove? Other times the subject changes but the ending feels strangely familiar. [Lindsay Gibson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) writes about that kind of repeated pattern in her work on emotional immaturity: you bring up something that hurt you and somehow your part of it is gone by the end.

Unlike most other psychedelics, 5-MeO-DMT is extremely dangerous. Even taking 1/3 too much for you might be deadly, or permanently mind-shattering (according to a personal conversation I had with the admin of 5meodmt.org years ago). If combined with drugs that boost dopamine or serotonin (or MAOIs like in ayahuasca/harmalas/caapi/rue), the venom/5-MeO-DMT becomes much more deadly, but that doesn't stop certain people from promoting this risky combination. Make sure you investigate interactions between all the meds and supplements you take before using 5-MeO-DMT.

There's a question I keep coming back to with inner work: am I actually processing something, or am I checking whether I've processed it? The hurt can be completely real either way. But if you're back at the same wound for the hundredth time mostly to see whether you've finally grieved it correctly, the healing itself can become the hook.

Don't be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that's the endgame, it's just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy, just like real growing up is not something you do forever. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn't as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

If closing your eyes starts making the room disappear, open them and look around. Of course, the point isn't that closed eyes are bad; it's whether you still know where you are, what time it is, and can feel your body here. You're not trying to prove anything by staying in it. If these sessions keep leaving you more disoriented, more compelled, or less able to function afterward, make them shorter and get some grounded support.

Write the furious version somewhere private. I'm serious: if twelve sentences are already screaming to get out, pretending you have only two civilized ones probably won't make you wiser. Just don't send it yet. Come back when you've cooled off a little and see what's still true. Maybe you were unfair. Maybe you also finally said no. Keep the no. Add the apology if you owe one. The useful reply might be shorter, or there might not be one. If you say you'll answer tomorrow, mean tomorrow.

You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they. If they promise to change, that's probably as useful as their prior promises were. Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy. Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise? Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.

It is good that there are some drugs like ketamine and 5-MeO-DMT which can help people with super fortified egos to go beyond their ego. Unfortunately, what usually ends up happening with such super dissociating drugs is something called "Spritual Bypassing," in which people avoid doing the inner child reparenting therapy to heal their traumas, and instead they use a drug like this, or even spirituality in general, to completely dissociate and dis-identify with all their traumas.

Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships. Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn’t opened it. That drove me crazy. Why would she lie like that? But looking back on it now, I could have just seen it as some kind of mental illness rather than "lying" since there was no strategy behind it, and in fact she was usually quite honest.

The first draft is often the part of me that got hurt grabbing the pencil first. I don't want the adult to snatch it away because what came out was angry or messy or not especially skillful. Usually there was something real underneath it that I was trying to get across: this hurt, I need you to understand what happened, I need you to stop doing that, I need some help here. The adult can sit beside the child, keep his hand on the pencil, and help him find a way to say it that the other person might actually hear. But that's a different job from taking care of the person who wrote the first version. Maybe he needs protection, maybe reassurance, maybe actual help. Making the message better doesn't mean deciding the protest itself was childish just because it came out badly.

One awful conversation can leave you pretty certain you've finally figured somebody out. Then they come back later and actually deal with what you raised. They may still disagree with you, and you may still hate the boundary they're holding. One fight can be awful without being the whole pattern. [Lindsay Gibson's work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) on emotional immaturity looks at what keeps happening across different conversations.
